passage:
Monday: Kalyani, twelve, had a history project due on Friday. She watched cartoons instead. "Tomorrow," she said.
Wednesday: Nothing done. Her friend Arohi offered her own finished project to copy. "Just change the colours." Kalyani's stomach twisted. She wanted to say yes. She said, "No. I'll do mine," and stayed up late drawing a messy map.
The next week: She got a C and a comment: "Rushed but honest." That Sunday she stuck a small timetable above her desk: thirty minutes each evening, cartoons after. For the next project she started on day one.

qa.q: What did Arohi offer Kalyani?
qa.a: Her own finished project to copy.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani's stomach twist when Arohi made the offer?
qa.a: She was tempted because she was behind, but she felt that copying would be wrong.

qa.q: What change did Kalyani make, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: A small daily timetable with cartoons after work, which stops the last-minute rush.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel when Kalyani says no?
qa.a: Perhaps a little surprised or awkward about offering, but she may respect Kalyani's choice.

grounding: It shows a girl moving from procrastination through a cheating temptation to an honest study routine.

passage: Omkar, you want to hear about the exam hall? When I was twelve, a boy passed me a chit with the maths answers and whispered, "Irfan, take it." The invigilator was looking out of the window. My heart was banging. I hadn't studied much; I'd played marbles all week. I pushed the chit back without opening it. I got 41 out of 100, and my father was quiet for a whole day. But that night I made a rule for myself: one hour of study before marbles, every day. The next year I got 78. And I never had to wonder whether the marks were really mine.

qa.q: What did young Irfan score in that maths exam?
qa.a: 41 out of 100.

qa.q: What was young Irfan feeling in the moment the heart started banging?
qa.a: Irfan was scared and tempted, knowing Irfan hadn't studied and that using the chit would be cheating.

qa.q: Which choice in the exam hall turned out to matter most, and why?
qa.a: Pushing the chit back unopened; the low mark hurt, but it led to Irfan's daily study rule and marks that were truly Irfan's own.

qa.q: How might Irfan's father have felt about the 41 out of 100?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed, since he stayed quiet for a whole day, though he did not know Irfan had refused to cheat.

grounding: It shows, told by an elder, a child refusing to cheat after slacking and then building a steady study habit.

passage: It was exam week, and the house next door was hosting a wedding: drums until midnight, lights flashing through the window. Parul, eleven, kept to her plan anyway: up at six when it was quiet, revise for an hour, reach school on time. Her cousin Ankita, visiting for the wedding, begged, "Come to the mehendi, just skip tonight's revision." Parul looked at her timetable. "I'll come after I finish chapter four." She stuffed cotton wool in her ears, finished by nine, then went and danced for an hour. The next morning she was still at the bus stop by seven.

qa.q: What time did Parul get up to revise?
qa.a: At six, when it was quiet.

qa.q: Why did Parul look at her timetable before answering Ankita?
qa.a: She felt torn between joining the fun and sticking to her plan, so she checked how she could do both.

qa.q: Which of Parul's choices shows a good balance?
qa.a: Finishing chapter four before joining the celebration let her keep her routine and still enjoy the wedding.

qa.q: How might Ankita see Parul's choice?
qa.a: She may think Parul is too strict, but she gets her cousin at the mehendi in the end.

grounding: It shows a girl keeping a diligent, punctual study routine despite a noisy wedding and a tempting invitation.

passage: At 7:40, in the lobby of their building in Pune, Devika held out her maths notebook. 'Just copy the last four. The bus comes in ten minutes.' Yogesh looked at the neat columns. He had left the sums for last night and then watched cartoons till dinner. His fingers actually touched the notebook. Then he pushed it back. 'Ma'am will call me to do one on the board, and I'll stand there like a statue.' He sat on the steps and did two sums fast and messily, and wrote 'will finish at lunch' beside the rest. On the bus he muttered, 'Tonight, sums before cartoons.' Devika shrugged, but she put her notebook back in her bag.

qa.q: What time was it when Devika offered her notebook?
qa.a: It was 7:40.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh push the notebook back after touching it?
qa.a: He was tempted, but he worried about being asked to solve a sum on the board, and he seemed to know copying would not fix his delay.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do so this morning rush does not happen again?
qa.a: He could stick to his own plan of sums before cartoons, doing homework soon after school.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt when he refused?
qa.a: She may have felt a little brushed off, but her shrug and putting the notebook away suggest she accepted it.

grounding: Shows a child tempted to copy after putting off homework, choosing honest partial work and a new routine.

passage:
'Pooja, isn't the volcano model due Monday?'
'Papa, it's only Friday.'
'And tomorrow is Nani's birthday lunch. And Sunday you have dance.'
'...Oh.'
'So when were you planning to build it?'
'I thought Wasim was doing most of it.'
'Is that what Wasim thinks?'
Pooja picked at the sofa cushion. 'He did the drawing last week. I said I'd do the clay.'
'Then the clay is yours.'
'Can't you just make it tonight? You're good at this.'
'I'll sit with you. Your hands, though, not mine.'
She groaned, then went to find the clay. 'Fine. But you hold the bottle when we test it.'
'Deal. Call Wasim first and tell him honestly where it stands.'

qa.q: When is the volcano model due?
qa.a: It is due on Monday.

qa.q: What does Pooja picking at the cushion suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She likely felt a bit guilty as she realised she had not done her share of the project.

qa.q: How did Papa support her without doing the work for her?
qa.a: He helped her see how little time was left and offered to sit with her, but insisted on her own hands and on being honest with Wasim.

qa.q: If you were Wasim, what would you want from Pooja?
qa.a: I would want her to do the clay she promised and tell me honestly if she was behind, so Monday is not a surprise.

grounding: Shows a child's procrastination on a shared project and a parent steering her toward doing her own part honestly.

passage: I'm Yash, and in Class 6 I left my science project until the last night. I told myself I'd start every day for three weeks. Then the night before, I panicked. My friend Vikas messaged, "Copy mine, change the colours." I nearly did. But I thought about Sir's face if he found out, and about how I'd feel handing it in. I stayed up and made a bad one myself. It got a C. Since then I do twenty minutes every evening, even when I don't feel like it.

qa.q: What grade did Yash's project get?
qa.a: It got a C.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling the night before the project was due?
qa.a: Yash felt panicked and tempted to copy, but also uneasy about cheating.

qa.q: What would you advise Yash for the next big project?
qa.a: Break it into small daily parts from the first week, like his new twenty-minute habit.

qa.q: What might Vikas have been thinking when he offered his project?
qa.a: He probably wanted to help his friend, not realising it was dishonest.

grounding: Shows a child choosing honest work over copying after procrastinating, and building a study routine.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Kishore, November
Damini (11) has been on time every day this month, which is new for her. She now does homework in the library before the bus. During Tuesday's test, the boy beside her left his answer sheet uncovered while he went to sharpen a pencil. I saw Damini turn her paper over and look away until he returned. She got a lower mark than him, but it was her own. I've told her privately that I noticed, and I'll mention her new routine to her parents.

qa.q: What did Damini do when the boy's answer sheet was uncovered?
qa.a: She turned her paper over and looked away until he returned.

qa.q: What might Damini have felt when she saw the uncovered sheet?
qa.a: She may have been tempted but chose honesty, feeling it mattered more than the mark.

qa.q: Why was Kishore right to tell Damini privately that he noticed?
qa.a: It shows her honest choice is valued without embarrassing her in front of others.

qa.q: How might Damini's parents feel when they hear about her new routine?
qa.a: Proud and encouraged by the change in her punctuality and study habits.

grounding: Shows a child building punctuality and study routines and choosing academic honesty, noted by her teacher.

passage:
Yusuf's diary, Monday
Plan: homework at five. Reality: played cricket till seven. Then dinner. Then I was tired. My sister Farida saw my face and said, "Timer, little brother." We set it for twenty-five minutes. No talking. I did the English worksheet and half the maths. Then a five-minute break. Then the other half. Done by nine. I hate admitting it, but the timer works. Tomorrow I'm doing homework at five before cricket. I'll write in here if I actually do it.

qa.q: How long did they set the timer for?
qa.a: Twenty-five minutes.

qa.q: What does Yusuf writing "I hate admitting it" suggest?
qa.a: Yusuf felt a bit sheepish but relieved that the timer helped to stop the putting-off.

qa.q: What small step would help Yusuf tomorrow?
qa.a: Start the timer at five before going out, so cricket becomes the reward after homework.

qa.q: How might Farida see Yusuf's evening?
qa.a: Farida probably feels pleased that the timer idea helped Yusuf get it done.

grounding: Shows a child noticing a habit of procrastination and trying a simple routine to study.

passage: In Kolar, the power went off at seven most evenings. Samir used it as an excuse: no light, no homework. His friend Pankaj lit a lantern and did his sums at the table every night, even when the others were playing outside. On Friday the test was on fractions, and Samir hadn't done any of the homework. Pankaj whispered, "Want to see mine?" Samir looked at the neat pages, then shook his head. "I'll just do badly." He did. That evening, when the power went, Samir asked Pankaj if he could share the lantern. "Fractions again?" "Fractions again," Samir said.

qa.q: When did the power go off most evenings?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he shook his head at Pankaj's pages?
qa.a: He felt tempted but also honest and a little ashamed about not having done the work.

qa.q: What could Samir try so the power cuts don't stop his homework?
qa.a: He could study with Pankaj by the lantern or do his homework before seven.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Samir asking to share the lantern?
qa.a: Pankaj likely feels happy and a bit proud that his friend wants to work with him now.

grounding: A boy in a small town stops using power cuts as an excuse and refuses to copy homework.

passage: In Singapore, Wei had a timetable taped above his desk: maths, then English, then a fifteen-minute break, every day after school. His classmate Leila leaned over in the canteen. "My brother kept last year's test. Same questions every year. Want a photo?" Wei hesitated. The test was tomorrow, and he was stuck on long division. "No," he said slowly. "If I just copy, I'll be stuck forever." Leila shrugged. That evening he worked through ten division problems, crossed out six, then got the last four right. He went to bed tired but calmer.

qa.q: How long was Wei's break on his timetable?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What was Wei feeling when he hesitated?
qa.a: He felt tempted and stressed, because the test was tomorrow and he was stuck.

qa.q: What could Wei do if he was still stuck on long division?
qa.a: He could ask his teacher or a parent for help, rather than using the old test.

qa.q: How might Leila see Wei's refusal?
qa.a: She seemed unbothered, but might wonder why he chose the harder way.

grounding: A boy in Singapore keeps his study routine and refuses to use last year's leaked test.

passage: The hostel study hour started at six sharp. Gautam, twelve, strolled in at quarter past for the third day in a row. Sonali Ma'am, the warden, didn't shout. She just wrote the time in her book. "Why are you always late?" she asked afterwards. "I lose track playing football." "What could help?" Gautam thought. "An alarm on my watch at quarter to six?" "Try it." The next day, he was the first one in, sweaty and panting, books open at six. Sonali Ma'am looked up and ticked her book.

qa.q: At what time did study hour start?
qa.a: At six sharp.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt when Sonali Ma'am wrote the time in her book?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and a bit guilty about being late again.

qa.q: What worked in Sonali Ma'am's approach?
qa.a: She asked Gautam to find his own solution instead of just punishing him.

qa.q: How might Sonali Ma'am see Gautam arriving first the next day?
qa.a: She would likely be pleased that his own plan worked.

grounding: A boy in a hostel stops coming late to study hour by setting his own alarm.

passage:
I'm Nitin, Pooja's older brother. This year, Pooja, twelve, changed.

Last year she did homework at midnight, crying. This year she made a timetable on the fridge: 5 to 6 homework, 6 to 6.30 play, 7 to 8 revision. She sticks to it, mostly.

Last month her friend offered to send her the answers for the science worksheet. I heard her on the phone: "No, I want to do it myself, or I won't know it for the test."

She got 16 out of 20 on the test. She seemed happy, but also said, "I lost marks on the diagram. I'll practise."

qa.q: What time does Pooja do revision?
qa.a: 7 to 8 revision.

qa.q: How did Pooja seem to feel after the test?
qa.a: Pooja seemed happy, though determined to improve the diagram.

qa.q: What study habits could Pooja keep building?
qa.a: She could stick to her timetable, keep doing her own work, and practise weak areas like diagrams.

qa.q: How does Nitin see Pooja's change?
qa.a: Nitin noticed the change from last year and seems impressed by her discipline and honesty.

grounding: An older brother observes his sister building a study routine and refusing to copy answers.

passage:
First week of summer holidays: Sharmila, eleven, puts off her holiday homework. "I have six weeks," she tells Minakshi. They play carrom all day.

Fourth week: Sharmila opens her bag and sees twenty pages undone. Her stomach sinks. She and Minakshi make a chart: two pages a day, then carrom.

Last week of holidays: Sharmila finishes the last page. She didn't copy Minakshi's answers, even when it was tempting. "Next time," she says, "I'll start the chart on day one."

qa.q: How many pages were undone in the fourth week?
qa.a: Twenty pages were undone.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when she saw the undone pages?
qa.a: Sharmila felt anxious and regretful, her stomach sinking.

qa.q: What helped Sharmila finish her work honestly?
qa.a: Making a daily chart with Minakshi and doing her own answers helped.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel helping Sharmila with the chart?
qa.a: Minakshi likely felt supportive and pleased to help her friend.

grounding: Over the summer holidays, a girl moves from procrastinating to a steady, honest study routine.

passage:
Pallavi, sit with your Arohi Dida. You want to copy your friend's project? Let me tell you something.

When I was twelve, during the Durga Puja holidays, we had to make a model of a village. My friend Tuku's elder brother made a beautiful one for her. I was jealous.

She said, "Copy mine, change the colours, no one will know."

I nearly did. But I thought, "Then it won't be mine." So I made my own: crooked huts from matchboxes and a pond from a broken mirror.

I got less marks than Tuku. But the teacher kept mine in the display cupboard, because it was clearly done by a child.

So, Pallavi, do it yourself. Even crooked.

qa.q: What did Arohi use to make the pond?
qa.a: She made a pond from a broken mirror.

qa.q: How did young Arohi feel when Tuku's brother made her model?
qa.a: Young Arohi felt jealous and tempted to copy.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Arohi's story?
qa.a: She decided not to copy because the work wouldn't be hers, and made her own crooked model.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen Arohi's model?
qa.a: The teacher valued it as honest work by a child, keeping it in the display cupboard.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at twelve, she chose honest effort over copying a friend's project.

passage: The science project was due the day after Durga Puja ended, and Vikas had spent the holidays at pandals. On the last evening, the power went out across their Kolkata neighbourhood. His friend Anirban texted: "Take my brother's old volcano project. Sir won't know." Vikas looked at the message for a long time. Then he lit two candles, opened his textbook and started drawing the water-cycle chart himself, in pencil. By midnight it was rough but finished. The next morning he handed it in and told Sir, "It's messy. I left it too late. Next time I'll start in week one." Sir nodded. "Honest and on time. Seven out of ten."

qa.q: What did Anirban offer Vikas?
qa.a: His brother's old volcano project.

qa.q: Why did Vikas look at Anirban's message for a long time?
qa.a: He was tempted by the easy way out but uneasy about cheating, torn between the two.

qa.q: What could Vikas change so the next project isn't a midnight rush?
qa.a: He could start in week one as he said, doing a small part each day even during the holidays.

qa.q: How might Sir see Vikas's rough chart and admission?
qa.a: Sir seems to value the honesty and punctuality more than neatness, and rewards it with seven out of ten.

grounding: Shows a child who put off a project choosing to finish it honestly by candlelight rather than copy.
